p: Sure. As far as language access at the agency, we have multilingual outreach staff. We also— I think we speak 16+ languages among our outreach team alone. You know, and then we also have access to a vendor that can provide language access services for the languages that we don't cover.
Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you.
Thank you. I have a couple of questions. I want to follow up on the vacancy. How many positions are associated with the NYC Office of Talent and Workforce Development? In FY26 and FY27?
It's— I believe that's about 40 positions.
40 positions that are accounted for, and how many of those are vacant?
I'm not sure exactly that breakdown.
We'll follow up with you, Chair. I think it's over 10.

Okay, thank you. Moving on to Executive Order 11. On January 14th, the mayor issued Executive Order 11 directing city agencies to identify ways to cut costs and simplify regulations for small businesses. You are one of seven agencies under the direction of Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Justice working to cut red tape for small businesses. The deadline to create a full inventory of the fees and civil penalties collected by the agencies and whether they could be reduced was due in late February. Did SBS have any fees or penalties that could be reduced?
No, we're not a regulatory agency, Chair.
Are you aware of any fees to-date or penalties that have been identified that could be reduced for small businesses across the board?

We have the inventory of fees and penalties from the partner city agencies. We are currently reviewing that and hope to

come to City Council with legislative proposals for how to move forward.

Okay, thank you. Going into— and Council Member Lee alluded to the funds, the New York City Future Fund. So on March 17th, the Mamdani administration announced a city-backed loan program aimed at improving access to affordable financing for small businesses. Funding of $80 million is expected in a future financial plan. The program lowers barriers by reducing minimum loan sizes, cutting interest rates, and offering more flexible repayment terms tied to business revenue. It specifically targets underserved entrepreneurs, including immigrant, minority, and women-owned businesses. With the New York City Future Fund lowers minimum loan sizes to $25,000 and eligibility revenue to $50,000. How many additional businesses does SBS project will now qualify for these loans?
We hope to serve 1,000 businesses, Chair.
Over what timeframe?
100 businesses annually. So over a 10-year time period.
And how does this fund differ from existing grants that SBS provides to businesses?
This is the first loan product that is specifically tied to revenue.

Speaking of revenue, the new fund reduces the monthly repayment rates from a flat 9.5 percent of revenue to as low as two percent of monthly revenue depending on loan size and business needs. Can you tell a little more about how that criteria will be used and how the department is managing the risk of these loans?
So we work in partnership with CDFIs, and there's our underwriting team that’s at the lender that's monitoring this closely.
And also, we had piloted it, and that's part of what– of the analysis that took place in the pilot program that preceded the launch.
Is the pilot specific to any particular type of business, any particular area of the city?

No. The thing that makes the program unique is for businesses that don't have an even revenue stream. So like a seasonal business. So that's what makes it different. Typically when you're getting a loan for a small business, you're gonna have a fixed monthly repayment rate, and there's a certain segment of businesses. The easiest example, I think, is the seasonal business where in the high season you're making a lot of revenue, but in the low season you're not able to pay that fixed rate. So what makes this program unique is that the payment that the small business makes back every month is calibrated to the revenue that they're taking in. And so that's kind of— there was— that was part of the pilot. That was part of kind of the buildup to this was to kind of design that underwriting, design the technology, design the program components so that every month that payment gets calculated based on how much the business is actually making.
And then will any part of this fund be issued in the term– as grants versus a loan?
No, it's all– it's all loan.

Okay. And speaking of technology, how easy is it for a business to get access to these loans? Like, today, some loan products, you can go online and in two minutes, you know, if you're approved and the funds are in your account in 48 hours. How— what is the time frame for a business in need to request and receive funding?

There is an application process. It can be done online. We also strongly, strongly encourage and connect anyone applying to the loans— for the loans— to a small business advisor. And what we found is the success rate of businesses applying for the loans is much, much higher when they work with an advisor that we provide them. So that adds, you know, that adds a little bit of time to the process, but it's time well spent because it makes sure that, you know, the finances are right so that the loan is appropriate for the business and it positions them for success.
And then are these advisors all— advisors, underwriters all under SBS or are you partnering with different CDFIs?
They work with our partner CDFIs and then also you can get this assistance at our Business Solution Centers as well.
Okay. Now, given the broader concerns about budget gaps, how will SBS ensure this program is financially sustainable over multiple years?
There's about $10 million of city seed funding in the program as well, in addition to our partnerships with private– with CDFIs and other private institutions.
And the program prioritizes immigrant, minority, and women-owned businesses. What specific outreach and eligibility safeguards are in place to ensure that these groups actually receive the funds?

So I think primarily, we're relying on our partnership with CDFIs who are in the community, know the businesses, and have those longstanding relationships in addition to other outreach that we at SBS are doing to inform the business owners about the program.
Going to other business assistance– financial awards to businesses dropped 10.4 percent year over year and significantly since fiscal year 2023. What are the primary drivers of this decline?

So we're very proud of the fact that we've served 488 businesses and facilitated over 563 awards in fiscal year '25, totaling $46 million. These are great results for small businesses here in New York City. The decrease you're seeing there is reflective of the reduced availability of low-interest lending capital, as federal COVID recovery funds have expired at the end of fiscal year 24. And I just want to point out, we're also meeting our targets as well.

Okay, at this time I will turn it over to Council Member Avilés. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Very, very kind Chair, thank you. So, just to follow up on the IS— on the IBSP's contract. My understanding is that the contract is in total worth $1.2 million. Is that correct?

Yes, that's correct.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yeah. And, and so in fact– I guess following up also on Council Member Morano's points is the whole change in structure, and you know, I think the thing that you had mentioned, that the desire is to move beyond industrial manufacturing providers. Is your intention to add additional resources to that contract, or will it remain the same?

Well, our intent is not to move beyond industrial providers, it’s to ensure that those services are available at all of our sites, and we encourage industrial providers– COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] And outreach, change the structure, but not add any new resources.
We encourage them to apply to the RFP. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay.

For sure. And make sure that their services are available. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay. I think the point, the point that want to drive here is this is a critical, very complex group of provide— of businesses, and if there is an interest in expanding

to touch more businesses, I think it wouldn't be counterintuitive to say we need additional resources rather than watering down the actual structure through the RFP. But I think we're going to— I have a list of questions that I want to follow up with you specifically about this. I wanted to ask a little bit about– congratulations on our– on the appointment of Carina Kaufman-Gutierrez and talk a little bit about street vendors. How much funding is allocated in fiscal 27 Preliminary Budget for the new Division of Street Vendor Assistance?

We're currently discussing with OMB funding and the resources needed as part of the exec plan, and those conversations are ongoing. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And how much are you anticipating in terms of staffing and resources that will be needed to launch this program?

So I think our previous fiscal impact statement right around the time when the bill was passed had it at eight staff lines totaling about $2.5, $2.8 million.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Are you targeting to expand the office meet the new mandates of increasing licensing?

Well, the mandates of increasing licensing, the resources we're requesting are to serve vendors. The licensing resources that would be needed to issue additional licenses would be at the agencies, at the licensing agencies. Here it would be DOHMH and DCWP. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Right. You hold another part of– a piece of the puzzle. In terms of– how much of the portion of SBS's budget will be dedicated in particular to street vendor outreach, given kind of the new licenses, which is really important?

So our intent is to use all the resources at SBS's current disposal, including the outreach team to make sure that folks are aware, the NYC Best team and others, to make sure that street vendors are aware that the licenses are available and to also hear from street vendors about what are the regulatory burdens that they're facing, right, that we can help tackle as part of EO 11 as well?

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great. This is, you know, important to us as another community that has so many immigrant— small business owners and our smallest business owners. It's important that we set it up for success and provide the resources really that it so desperately needs. Lastly, what is the— do you know what the per license administrative cost might be? And if SPS is ready to increase the volume of that?

We would have to defer to DOHMH and DCWP on what the administrative cost is per license and their capabilities to take on the additional volume. Just one more item that I wanted to point out with respect to street vendors is our new $750,000 challenge procurement that we're issuing to try to tackle some of the issues and provide additional services to street vendors. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Can you tell us a little bit more about it?
Sure.

Council Member, so this is a Venture Forward, which was our first challenge procurement. So unlike typical procurements where we lay out specifically what we want from

responders, this was an opportunity for us at the agency to listen to community stakeholders and others about innovative solutions that could help address some of the gaps we're seeing in street vendor services. So we were proud to issue that RFP in late— I think it was December of last year, and we're at the final stages of announcing the recipients of that work. And that work will be $750,000 spent this fiscal year with the opportunity to leverage that funding into the early months of the next fiscal year. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great, thank you so much. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. Council member Hanif?
Thank you. Could SBS confirm if the MENA community has been added to the disparity study?
Thank you for the question, Council Member. So, the study has concluded, and we're ready to brief you and any other council member in the next coming weeks on the results of the study.
Are you able to share anything as a preview right now?
No, unfortunately not right now.
Could you share what percentage of business—
Chair Hanif, can we share a little bit, a preview of something?
Love that.

So, one challenge, and we'll talk about it at our briefing as well. One challenge that came out of this initial work was the lack of citywide data, available data on the MENA community. And so we were proud that to address this for future analyses, we announced on January 14th the first ever self-identification option for businesses that register in the city's Passport system that unlocks a whole series of data points that previously did not exist, which hampered some of the analysis last year.
Well, that'll go a long way. Are you able to share what percentage of businesses are currently enrolled in SBS programs that are certified MWBEs?
What I can share is that, um, 75 percent of the businesses that received an MWBE contract benefited from SBS programming.
And the total number of businesses that are MWBEs?
It's about 11,000.
And is that a increase or decrease? What are the five-year goals or annual goals?
To increase, and it's a steady increase over the last five fiscal years.
Got it. Okay. And what targeted outreach does SBS do to reach minority and women-owned businesses in underserved communities?

So, one of the things we highlighted earlier was our contracting summit just two months ago where we brought MWBE businesses and contracting agencies together under one roof to help folks connect, and make sure that MWBE businesses are aware of the services that are– I'm sorry, of the contract opportunities that are available. That is in addition to our regular suite

of outreach offerings, which include webinars and, and our outreach team. I'm pounding the pavement and connecting with business owners.
And in events like that, how many businesses participate would you say?
Yeah, we– so we had 1,700 businesses participate, which is an all-time high for us.
And is there specific outreach and engagement funding associated with this work? No, no, this is built into our suite of programming.
Built-in, got it. What is SBS's relationship with Dining Out NYC?

So certainly through our Office of Nightlife and our food and beverage partnerships, we engage with restaurants here in New York City, and we're certainly supportive of the rumblings we've heard about extend— expanding the program and making it available year round. That's wonderful. Do— and I know that DOT manages the program and interfaces with the businesses. How does SBS participate?

So through the initial creation of the, you know, program, we advise DOT not only on the program guidelines, the requirements, but also on the user experience when a small business would approach the dining out application program. How are they experiencing the information that they're receiving? So we provided, um, our advice and consultation to the partners at DOT when they set up that initial program. And currently really excited at the mayor's support, the speaker's support, and DOT commissioner's support for an upgraded program that's year-round that would solve a lot of the application requirements and other burdensome challenges that some businesses have been complaining about, which has impacted participation throughout the city, including in your district.
Exactly. And so that means you all are assessing and evaluating what DOT might be hearing about the challenges in the program.

We've been sharing some of the challenges that we hear from our stakeholders to DOT, and also really excited to leverage this Executive Order 11 opportunity that the

mayor has laid out to cut fines and fees, to further evaluate if there are items that we can advance before the larger legislative proposal process on outdoor dining.

Got it. And I want to ask about BIDs. I don't know, have they been asked? Does the agency believe that there are enough positions to carry out the agency's goals when it comes— oh wait, not BIDs, BID containerization is what I wanted to ask about. Has SBS been in contact with DSNY regarding the BID containerization requirements, and what concerns are you hearing?

We've been in contact with DSNY through the policymaking process and made sure— connected them very early on to the bid association and BID leaders so they could understand the operational impacts on businesses and, and BIDs to comply. We know that the City Council and the administration last year, the former administration last year, committed funding for containerization for bids. We've heard that bids have leveraged that funding to attempt to comply with the rules of DSNY on containerization.
And you all believe that the $5 million that's allocated is substantial?
We haven't heard any BID suggest to us that they've now had a funding challenge in containerization with the availability of those DSNY grants.
Great. And then when complaints arise or challenges arise, do they interface with DSNY or SBS?

So the Bid Network has always been able to reach out to us. We're— we sit on the board of directors for each of the bids, so we definitely hear complaints throughout their experience working with city agencies. But we also are proud that DSNY has really built really strong relationships with the BID partners, and have their own open lines of communication. Wonderful. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. I do have a quick follow-up in terms of MWBEs, um, being awarded contracts. How do you set your targets? Because you guys have set targets at approximately 1,200– a little over 1,200, but exceed them quite frequently. So how are those targets set?
I think it's based just— I think those are historical and they're set in partnership with the Mayor's Office of Operations the PMMR targets. So yeah.
So do they kind of carry over year to year, or is there disparity study or some type of assessment every few years to see if the goals need to be increased?
Well–
[interposing] Decreased.

I mean, our goal is always to surpass and exceed the targets. The targets themselves and the p.m., they do carry over year to year. But for us, you know, we look at previous year's performance, and that's the number we try to exceed. And that's why we've seen that steady increase over the last five fiscal years.

I would like to acknowledge that Council Member Brewer has joined us. And while we are speaking of MWBEs, Council Member Brooks Powers, who is on Zoom, has a question. According to this year's comptroller's report, only 5.3 percent of the city's contract value was directed

to MWBEs. How is SBS working with the city to promote further MWBE utilization?

So, I can't speak to the comptroller's numbers, but for us we– you know, I think the number of registrants year over year increased leasing speaks to our commitment to making sure that there are more MWBEs registered with the city. I think in the last fiscal year, we directed— was it two point— I'm sorry, $6.9 billion in contracts to MWBEs, which we're very proud of. That's where our focus is, is to making sure that the businesses are able to register, have what they need, and can access the city funding.
And to help with that, is part of that to work with more of the agencies to make sure that they're using or reaching out to the MWBE community?

Certainly we try to do our part, but we also rely on the Office of MWBE's within the mayor's office to communicate to the city agencies and set the citywide policy. I mean, just this last fiscal year, I believe the— we achieved the 36 percent MWB utilization, which is a new record,

and we're very proud of that work. And kudos to the Office of MWBEs as well.
What system, or how do you guys– what data is used, like, which system is used to track the data, and is it consistent across the agencies?
We use the Passport system.
Are you familiar with B2G at all? Okay. Is that something that you guys get data from, or—
OMWBE, the Office of MWBE at City Hall, is in the process of rolling out B2G to city agencies to also track other layers of data in addition to Passport.

Okay. Just trying to figure out how we can make sure that we're getting consistent data across the city of New York, where some numbers are here, some numbers are there. We're trying to figure out if we're in line to use one cohesive system that tracks everything across

Yes. So, the existing systems were Passport, and there's efforts

being made to also adapt B2G as an additional tracking mechanism.
Okay. And I see that certification rates have increased slightly since last year. What does the agency do— plan on doing to keep increasing the number of firms certified?

Yeah, we want to make sure that businesses are aware of the MWE program. So far in fiscal year 26, we've held 60 webinars and presentations just to get the information out there, you know, with our community partners across the city. And then that's really our focus. We think that, you know, the merits of the program are strong,that, you know, once we can bridge that gap and get the information to the businesses that it'll increase participation.

Okay. And one last question from Council Member Brooks-Powers. This administration has committed to cutting red tape and reducing unnecessary fines and fees for small businesses. What specific requirements or measure is SBS looking to change in the coming months?

We're taking a kind of all of the above approach. I mean, we're looking at time spent to– from business initiation to obtaining a license. You know, Dining Out NYC is another one that we're looking at just to ensure that, you know, especially in time for the summer season, that businesses are able to get the permits that they need to be able to partake in that program. So we're taking it across the board approach and look at city regulations.
Thank you. Council Member Brewer?

Thank you very much. I have a couple questions just on vacant stores. I know XYZ, you have a contract with them thanks to Blaze, I assume. And so my question is, does that continue? My district– I mean, there's so many vacant stores, and I assume it's across the city. So my question is– we can have the data, which is what we have, but what are we doing about it, if anything? Now, you know, we can— it's good to have opportunities for new stores, but if they can't do the rent or there's no— what are we doing about vacancy? That's number one. Number two is, is there

something that can be done with AI in terms of— I'm a big supporter of it— in terms of some of the work that you're doing? It seems to me that there is, but I'd love to hear from you. I'd like to also know the federal changes to the– federal SBA are horrible in terms of those who are immigrants not able to get a loan. So what are you doing to be able to support them? That's the backbone of our city in terms of replacing lost SBA financing. And then finally, I have a bill that passed a while ago, just making sure language— when I go talking to business, there's always a language issue, and it's even more prevalent around the city. So how are you making sure that you have all the different languages? Because if you don't understand something and you're getting a fine or fee in a language you don't understand, then that's going to be a problem. So my vacant stores, I have hundreds and hundreds and they're all across the city.

Sure. So let me tackle those, attempt to tackle them in order. So first with the vacancy data, we do still continue to contract with XYZ. I believe that's an OTI contract. As far as, as what can be done to try to, you know,

get business owners into those vacant storefronts, there's a couple of things that come to mind. I think first is our commercial lease assistance program. You know, we seek to help business owners by providing legal services to help them negotiate their lease, or if they're already in a storefront to just to remain there, providing assistance on renewing their leases. I think Executive Order 11 also is key here, just to ensure that businesses can quickly go from idea to actually being able to open their doors to business and doing what we can to cut the red tape. So those are some of the approaches that we're taking to make it easier for businesses and make sure that those vacant storefronts don't remain vacant for long. On AI, definitely something that we're looking at. Just last week, we launched an AI Unlocked training series. This is designed for businesses that are seeking to adopt, expand, or optimize their use of AI. These courses include introduction to AI skills that can help businesses streamline daily operations, automate tasks, and boost overall efficiency. I think there's more that we can do there, but that's just a snapshot of our approach here. On federal SBA loans, we share your concern,

Council Member. You know, over 50 percent of small businesses in New York City are immigrant-owned and operated. I think at SBS and under the leadership of Mayor Mamdani, we're taking a completely different approach. Just last week we announced the launching of the NYC Future Fund, right? Which is an affordable loan product for businesses whose revenue fluctuates seasonally, to ensure that a bad season doesn't mean that they have to then shutter their doors. We also continue our efforts to connect businesses to responsible and affordable financing with the NYC Funds Finder, initiative that we have here. And I think I answered all the questions.
Yeah, I think– I mean, the issue— language, language.

Oh yes, of course. So, you know, we mentioned earlier, among our executive team, we speak over 16 languages. So language access is huge and top of mind for us. And then we also tap into citywide resources through vendors to make sure that we're able to provide–

[interposing] And in terms of tourism, this maybe hasn't been answered, but what we're doing is we're bringing all the

concierges from the hotels to the Upper West Side so that they get a sense when somebody says, what should I do today? I know you all want them to go to Queens or Brooklyn. Hell no. I want them in Manhattan. So, I'm just saying, what else are we doing for the tourism in general, but obviously the big ones this summer, for the business?
So, definitely I think that the highest leverage opportunity upcoming this summer is the World Cup.
Right. No, that's what I mean, World Cup on this and the boats, those are the two things.
Yeah.
You got the boats too.
So–
[interposing] Sail 250. Yep.

Right. So we are in close contact with our community partners, including the BIDs, to make sure that small businesses can partake in these opportunities. Actually, this Wednesday, we have a briefing to which we've invited

all of our small business partners with the World Cup Czar, Maya Honda, to discuss other opportunities. We have a landing page for small businesses that are interested in learning more about how they can leverage the World Cup, the nyc.gov/ready— game ready
We have an Intro 90 to talk about these vacant stores, just so you know. You could look at it, right? Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member.
Thank you, Council Member. Going back to the NYC Future Fund for a moment. Will the $10 million in seed city money be in the Executive Budget?
It— we already have it. It was funded a couple of plans ago.
Okay, and then the $70 million in— is that all private money? Will that be–

[interposing] It leverages other lending capital, yes. So that's the City seed money that leverages the

remaining funds. And we also have $1 million in philanthropy.
And which plan will that be in?
No plan, because the $1 million is from philanthropy. The other lending capital does not flow through the city. It's through our partners.
So the $70 flows through–
[interposing] the $10 million that enables the whole program.
Okay, so $10 million city. The $70 flows through the CDFIs, and the $1 million is philanthropy.
Correct.
Okay.

And look– you know, it's completely scalable on that $10 million investment. If there are other lending partners out there that want to come in, if there are other philanthropy that wants to come in, we can

support it off of that base $10 million investment. So the program is completely scalable.
Okay, thank you. You mentioned the website, Game Ready. How has this been promoted? Council Member, that's why I asked. It's— this is my first time, too.
So definitely we've been promoting it to all of our partners, BIDs, and anytime we have a briefing with folks we've been promoting the website to help drive traffic to there.

One of our most common ways where businesses reach and access some of our programming is email marketing. It's been one of the most successful way that businesses sign up. So we've also promoted Game Ready NYC across all of our email marketing campaigns to the business clients that we work with. And the plan is to host webinars. We've been coordinating with the World Cup Czar team and also the host committee to try to land on a cadence and schedule that works for a lot of those partners. But once they do, the plan is for three to four webinars right leading up to the World Cup.
